Bayesian inference needs integrals over the posterior distribution of the model parameters. Earlier chapters computed them in closed form for simple models, for example Bayesian linear regression with a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian likelihood (Chapter 5). The posterior is then Gaussian, so we can compute with it directly or draw samples with standard packages. Models with non-linearities, hierarchical structures (Section 6.5) or complex priors quickly lose their closed forms. Even modest departures from the simple cases make the computation harder.

Bayes’ theorem gives the posterior up to a normalization constant \[ p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\theta}), \] where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are the parameters and \(\mathcal{D}\) is the data.

The unnormalized posterior is often not enough for practical use. Most questions in Bayesian inference ask for an expectation with respect to the posterior \[ \mathbb{E}[f(\boldsymbol{\theta})] = \int f(\boldsymbol{\theta}) p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathcal{D}) \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}, \]where \(f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is a function of the parameters. These integrals arise when we predict new observations, summarize parameter values or integrate out the nuisance parameters that we do not need to report.

We often chose Gaussian distributions and linear transformations because they are easy to handle mathematically. Logistic regression has a non-linearity, which made its posterior much harder to obtain. We could write down the unnormalized posterior, but we could not easily sample from it without approximations. We used the Laplace approximation for the posterior and the probit function in place of the logistic function for predictions (Chapter 9). These approximations become inadequate as models grow more complex.

Monte Carlo methods approximate these expectations with samples. If we can generate samples \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(2)}, \ldots, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(N)}\) from the target distribution \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathcal{D})\), the posterior that we want to describe, then \[ \mathbb{E}[f(\boldsymbol{\theta})] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(i)}). \]We used this idea earlier when we estimated means and variances from finite samples. Those estimates are simple Monte Carlo approximations, with the observed data as the samples.

The approximation becomes more accurate as the number of samples \(N\) increases. By the law of large numbers, a sample average approaches the expectation as \(N \to \infty\). By the central limit theorem, the error decreases in proportion to \(1/\sqrt{N}\), written \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})\), as for the sample mean (Section 3.6). This rate does not depend on the dimension, which helps for the high-dimensional parameter spaces of many astronomical models.

The name “Monte Carlo” comes from the casino in Monaco and refers to the role of chance. Scientists of the Manhattan Project coined it in the 1940s, when they used these methods for nuclear physics calculations.

Monte Carlo approximation works for any distribution from which we can generate samples. These methods do not depend on a particular model and serve regression, classification and clustering alike. We therefore need effective methods to generate samples from complex distributions. We study four ways to obtain samples or expectations. They are the grid approach, the inverse cumulative distribution function (CDF) method, rejection sampling and importance sampling.

12.1 Historical Context

People used random experiments to answer mathematical questions long before computers existed. One of the earliest examples is the needle experiment of Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, from the 18th century.

The experiment estimates the constant \(\pi\) from random physical events. We drop needles of length \(L\) on a floor with parallel lines spaced a distance \(T\) apart, where \(L \leq T\). By counting the needles that cross a line, we estimate \(\pi\) without any complex calculation.

Two random variables describe where a needle lands. The first is the perpendicular distance \(x\) from the center of the needle to the nearest line, with \(0 \leq x \leq T/2\). The second is the angle \(\theta\) between the needle and the lines, with \(0 \leq \theta < \pi\).

The two variables are independent and uniformly distributed. The distance \(x\) is uniform over \([0, T/2]\) with probability density \(2/T\), and the angle \(\theta\) is uniform over \([0, \pi]\) with probability density \(1/\pi\). A needle crosses a line when \(x\) is at most half the projection of the needle onto the perpendicular direction, that is when \[ x \leq \frac{L}{2}\sin\theta. \]The probability of crossing is then \[\begin{aligned} p(\text{crossing}) &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{L}{2}\sin\theta} \frac{2}{T} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{L\sin\theta}{T\pi} \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\ &= 2 \frac{L}{\pi T}. \end{aligned}\]

This result connects the probability of a crossing to the value of \(\pi\). We drop \(N\) needles in total and observe \(n_{\rm c}\) crossings. The empirical probability is \(n_{\rm c}/N\), and setting it equal to the theoretical probability gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{n_{\rm c}}{N} &\approx 2 \frac{L}{\pi T} \\ \pi &\approx 2 \frac{L}{T} \frac{N}{n_{\rm c}}. \end{aligned}\]

Figure 12.1 shows a simulated experiment that illustrates two principles that remain central to Monte Carlo methods. First, random sampling estimates a quantity that would otherwise need complex calculations, here \(\pi\). Second, the estimate becomes more accurate as the number of needles \(N\) increases, but the error decreases only as \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})\).

Buffon’s experiment and modern sampling rely on the same principle, random samples that approximate an integral. Buffon used a physical experiment out of necessity. A computer generates random numbers much faster.

12.2 The Grid Approach

The grid approach turns the continuous problem of sampling from a distribution into a discrete problem that we solve by counting, as in Buffon’s experiment. It replaces the distribution by a histogram, which introduces an approximation. The approximation vanishes as the grid becomes infinitely fine.

A pinball machine illustrates the idea. A ball drops from the top, bounces through a series of pegs and lands in one of several bins at the bottom. Each bin collects balls with a frequency proportional to the number of paths that lead to it. In sampling, the bins are grid points, and the frequency in a bin corresponds to the probability of the grid point.

Consider a random variable \(X\) with probability density function (PDF) \(p(x)\) on a bounded domain \([a, b]\). We divide the domain into \(n\) intervals of equal width, which gives the \(n+1\) grid points \[ x_i = a + i\Delta x, \quad i = 0, 1, \ldots, n, \] where \(\Delta x = (b-a)/n\) is the grid spacing.

At each grid point \(x_i\) we evaluate the PDF, \(p_i = p(x_i)\). These values do not sum to 1, so we normalize them. The normalization constant is \(Z = \sum_{i=0}^{n} p_i\), and the normalized probabilities are \(\tilde{p}_i = p_i/Z\). They are the probability masses of the grid points. Together they form a histogram approximation of the PDF.

Sampling from this discrete distribution is now straightforward. We partition the unit interval \([0,1]\) into segments with lengths proportional to the probabilities \(\tilde{p}_i\).

For this we compute the cumulative probabilities \[ s_i = \sum_{j=0}^{i} \tilde{p}_j, \quad i = 0, 1, \ldots, n. \]The cumulative probabilities are thresholds \(\{s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_n\}\) with \(s_0 = \tilde{p}_0\) and \(s_n = 1\). The sampling procedure has three steps.

  1. Generate a uniform random number \(u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)\), which means that intervals of equal length in \([0,1]\) have equal probability.

  2. Find the index \(i\) with \(s_{i-1} < u \leq s_i\).

  3. Return \(x_i\) as the sample.

This procedure ensures that the probability of sampling any grid point \(x_i\) is \(\tilde{p}_i\), as required.

Bimodal Gaussian Mixture Example

Consider a mixture of two Gaussians \[ p(x) = 0.7 \cdot \mathcal{N}(x | -2, 0.5^2) + 0.3 \cdot \mathcal{N}(x | 2, 1^2). \]This distribution has two modes. The dominant mode at \(x = -2\) is narrower and taller, and the secondary mode at \(x = 2\) is broader and shorter. We could sample from the mixture by selecting a component with probabilities equal to the mixture weights (Section 11.5) and then sampling from that Gaussian. The grid approach samples directly from the mixture. Figure 12.2 shows the grid, the thresholds and three samples for a coarse grid of \(n = 20\) intervals.

The grid approach handles the two modes, provided that the grid resolution is fine enough to resolve the features of the distribution.

Extension to Multiple Dimensions

The grid approach extends to several dimensions, but the number of grid points grows quickly. For a \(D\)-dimensional random variable \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_D)\) with joint PDF \(p(\mathbf{x})\), the discretization produces a \(D\)-dimensional grid \[ \mathbf{x}_{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_D} = (a_1 + i_1\Delta x_1, a_2 + i_2\Delta x_2, \ldots, a_D + i_D\Delta x_D), \] where \(i_j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n_j\}\) for each dimension \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, D\).

We evaluate the joint PDF at each grid point and normalize over all grid points. The sampling procedure is then the same as in the one-dimensional case.

The Curse of Dimensionality

The main limit of the grid approach is the curse of dimensionality. With \(n\) grid points per dimension, the number of grid points scales as \(n^D\), which grows exponentially with the dimension \(D\). The grid approach is therefore not feasible in high dimensions.

With 100 grid points per dimension, a one-dimensional problem needs 100 evaluations, a two-dimensional problem needs 10,000 and a five-dimensional problem needs 10 billion. At ten dimensions, the grid has \(10^{20}\) points, far more than we can evaluate in practice. The grid approach remains practical in one or two dimensions.

The grid approach also has a discretization error, because the samples are restricted to the grid points. This error may be too large for applications that need precise samples from the continuous distribution. A finer grid reduces the error, but in high dimensions the number of grid points grows exponentially. This trade-off between accuracy and computing time motivates more sophisticated methods.

12.3 Inverse CDF Method

The grid approach partitions the unit interval by probability masses and uses a uniform random number to pick a grid point. Let the grid spacing go to zero. The cumulative probabilities then become the CDF of the continuous distribution. The result is the inverse CDF method, also called inverse transform sampling, which samples from continuous distributions without discretization error.

For a random variable \(X\) with PDF \(p(x)\), the CDF \(F(x)\) is defined as \[ F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} p(t) \, \mathrm{d}t. \]The function \(F(x)\) is the probability that \(X\) takes a value less than or equal to \(x\). It has three properties that make it useful for sampling.

  • \(F(x)\) is non-decreasing, so \(F(x_1) \leq F(x_2)\) if \(x_1 < x_2\).

  • \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} F(x) = 0\) and \(\lim_{x \to \infty} F(x) = 1\).

  • For continuous distributions, \(p(x) = \mathrm{d}F(x)/\mathrm{d}x\).

The first two properties mean that the CDF maps the support of the distribution, the set of \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\), to the interval \([0,1]\). For example, the CDF of the standard Gaussian distribution is the function \(\Phi(x)\) of Section 9.6.

The inverse CDF method uses this map in reverse. If we can compute the CDF and find its inverse function, we generate samples by transforming uniform random numbers.

  1. Generate a uniform random number \(u \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)\).

  2. Compute \(x = F^{-1}(u)\), where \(F^{-1}\) is the inverse of the CDF.

  3. Return \(x\) as a sample from the distribution with CDF \(F\).

The CDF rises quickly where the PDF is high, because outcomes are likely there. It rises slowly where the PDF is low. In this way, equal probability mass maps to segments of equal length in \([0,1]\).

More formally, suppose that \(X\) has the CDF \(F_X(x)\), and define \(Y = F_X(X)\). We show that \(Y\) is uniform on \([0,1]\) by computing its CDF. For any \(y \in [0,1]\) \[\begin{aligned} P(Y \leq y) &= P(F_X(X) \leq y) \\ &= P(X \leq F_X^{-1}(y)) \\ &= F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) \\ &= y. \end{aligned}\]This is the CDF of a uniform distribution on \([0,1]\). The inverse CDF method uses this result in reverse. If \(U \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)\), then \(X = F_X^{-1}(U)\) follows the distribution with the CDF \(F_X(x)\).

We can also read the procedure on the plot of the CDF. A uniform random number \(u\) is a height on the vertical axis of the CDF plot. We move horizontally from height \(u\) to the CDF curve and project down to the horizontal axis, which gives the sample \(F^{-1}(u)\). Where the CDF is steep, the uniform heights are compressed on the horizontal axis and many samples fall there. Figure 12.3 shows this for the bimodal mixture.

Exponential Distribution

For the exponential distribution with PDF \(p(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x \geq 0\), the CDF is \[ F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}. \] Solving for \(x\) in terms of \(u = F(x)\) gives \[\begin{aligned} u &= 1 - e^{-\lambda x} \\ e^{-\lambda x} &= 1 - u \\ x &= -\frac{1}{\lambda} \ln(1-u). \end{aligned}\]Since \(1-u\) is also uniform on \([0,1]\) when \(u\) is uniform, we can simplify to \[ x = -\frac{1}{\lambda} \ln(u). \]

Power Law Distribution

Power law distributions appear frequently in astronomy. Examples are the mass function of stars, the distribution of galaxy luminosities and the energy distribution of cosmic rays. For a power law on \([x_{\min}, \infty)\) with PDF \(p(x) = (\alpha - 1)x_{\min}^{\alpha-1} x^{-\alpha}\) and \(\alpha > 1\), the CDF is \[ F(x) = 1 - \left(\frac{x_{\min}}{x}\right)^{\alpha-1}. \]Inverting this for \(x\) in terms of \(u = F(x)\) gives \[\begin{aligned} u &= 1 - \left(\frac{x_{\min}}{x}\right)^{\alpha-1} \\ \left(\frac{x_{\min}}{x}\right)^{\alpha-1} &= 1 - u \\ x &= x_{\min} (1-u)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}. \end{aligned}\]Again \(1-u \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)\) when \(u \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)\), so \[ x = x_{\min} u^{-\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}. \]

Advantages and Limitations

The inverse CDF method has three advantages over the grid approach. It generates samples from the target distribution with no discretization error. Each sample needs one uniform random number and one function evaluation, which is efficient when the inverse CDF is analytic. The inverse CDF method is also easy to implement for distributions with a known inverse CDF.

The inverse CDF method also has limits. It needs a closed form for the inverse CDF \(F^{-1}(u)\), which many distributions lack. Even when the CDF has a closed form, we may be unable to invert it analytically. A numerical inverse needs a root-finding algorithm for each sample, which can be expensive.

For multivariate distributions, the inverse CDF method meets additional difficulties. The CDF of \(D\) variables gives one number for a point with \(D\) coordinates. Many points give the same number, so one uniform random number \(u\) does not determine a point. The Rosenblatt transformation samples the first variable from its marginal distribution. It then samples each later variable from its conditional distribution. This needs all the conditional distributions and their inverses in closed form, which is rarely possible.

The inverse CDF method remains the method of choice when the inverse CDF is analytic. Libraries implement it for standard distributions, often with optimizations for numerical stability and speed. For many posterior distributions, in particular those from complex likelihoods or hierarchical models, it does not apply, so we need other approaches.

12.4 Rejection Sampling

The inverse CDF method gives exact samples, but it needs an analytic CDF and an analytic inverse. Many distributions in Bayesian inference and astronomical modeling have neither. Rejection sampling handles any distribution that we can evaluate, even when we cannot integrate or invert it analytically.

We accept or reject candidate points according to whether they fall under the curve of the target density.

Think of throwing darts at a board. We throw darts randomly at a rectangular region that contains the curve, keep the darts that land below the curve and discard the others. The kept darts follow the shape of the curve, because more darts land below it where it is high.

Let \(p(x)\) be the PDF of the target distribution. Rejection sampling uses a proposal distribution with PDF \(q(x)\) that has two properties.

  1. We can generate samples from \(q(x)\) efficiently.

  2. The scaled proposal covers the target. There is a constant \(M \geq 1\) such that \(M q(x) \geq p(x)\) for all \(x\) in the domain.

The second property makes \(p(x)/(M q(x))\) a valid acceptance probability, because this ratio lies between 0 and 1 for all \(x\).

The rejection sampling algorithm has four steps.

  1. Generate a sample \(x_* \sim q(x)\) from the proposal distribution.

  2. Compute the acceptance probability \(\alpha = p(x_*)/(M q(x_*))\).

  3. Generate a uniform random number \(u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)\).

  4. If \(u \leq \alpha\), accept \(x_*\) as a sample from \(p(x)\). Otherwise reject it and return to step 1.

Rejection sampling gives samples from \(p(x)\) because we accept each candidate \(x_*\) with the probability \(p(x_*)/(M q(x_*))\). Candidates where \(p(x_*)\) is large compared with \(q(x_*)\) are accepted more often, and candidates where it is small are rejected more often.

Geometric Interpretation

Rejection sampling works in a two-dimensional space, the domain of \(x\) and a vertical axis for the probability density. The scaled proposal \(M q(x)\) is an envelope above the target density. We generate the point \((x_*, u M q(x_*))\), where \(u\) is uniform between 0 and 1, and accept it if it falls below the target density curve. Points between the target density and the envelope are rejected. Figure 12.4 shows the accepted and rejected points for the bimodal mixture.

This is why rejection sampling is often described as “sculpting” the proposal distribution into the target. We start with samples from \(q(x)\) and keep those that follow the shape of \(p(x)\). The acceptance probability sets the fraction of candidates that we keep at each point.

Acceptance Rate and Efficiency

The efficiency of rejection sampling depends on the proposal distribution and on the constant \(M\). The expected number of iterations for one accepted sample equals \(M\). Equivalently, the acceptance rate, which is the fraction of candidates that we accept, equals \(1/M\). We therefore want \(M\) as small as possible while \(M q(x)\) stays above \(p(x)\).

The best proposal has the shape of the target, with \(M = 1\) and all samples accepted. This proposal needs samples from the target itself, which is the problem that we want to solve. In practice we balance ease of sampling, similarity to the target and coverage of the target by the scaled proposal.

Extension to Multiple Dimensions

Unlike the inverse CDF method, rejection sampling extends to many dimensions. For a \(D\)-dimensional target PDF \(p(\mathbf{x})\) we use a \(D\)-dimensional proposal PDF \(q(\mathbf{x})\) and follow the same procedure. Rejection sampling needs only values of the density, which may be known only up to a normalization constant. This suits Bayesian inference, where we can write the unnormalized posterior but cannot sample from it directly.

The Curse of Dimensionality

Rejection sampling becomes less efficient as the dimension increases, which is the curse of dimensionality. Consider a target and a proposal whose coordinates are independent and identically distributed, for example spherical Gaussians with different widths. If the acceptance rate in one dimension is \(c < 1\), then in \(D\) dimensions it is approximately \(c^D\). It decreases exponentially with the dimension.

Heavy tails cause a second problem. If the tails of \(p(x)\) decay more slowly than those of \(q(x)\), the constant \(M\) may be very large or infinite. For example, if \(p(x)\) has polynomial tails and \(q(x)\) has exponential tails, no finite \(M\) satisfies \(M q(x) \geq p(x)\) for all \(x\).

Even so, rejection sampling remains useful in low dimensions and when the target and the proposal match well. It also applies in many cases where the inverse CDF method fails.

12.5 Importance Sampling

The inverse CDF method and rejection sampling generate samples that follow the target distribution. Often we want only an expectation with respect to the target, such as a posterior mean or variance, and importance sampling estimates it directly.

Rejection sampling discards candidates, while importance sampling keeps all samples and weights each one to account for the difference between the proposal and the target. This can be more efficient for the same number of candidates.

Recall that many problems in Bayesian inference involve computing expectations of the form \[ \mathbb{E}_{p}[f] = \int f(x) p(x) \mathrm{d}x. \] Here \(f(x)\) is a function of interest and \(p(x)\) is the target PDF. If we could draw samples \(\{x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \ldots, x^{(N)}\}\) directly from \(p(x)\), we would approximate the expectation with the Monte Carlo estimator \[ \mathbb{E}_{p}[f] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x^{(i)}). \]

Importance sampling needs no samples from \(p(x)\). We sample from a different distribution \(q(x)\) that is easier to work with, and we correct the calculation.

We rewrite the expectation with the proposal distribution \(q(x)\) \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{p}[f] &= \int f(x) p(x) \mathrm{d}x \\ &= \int f(x) \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} q(x) \mathrm{d}x \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[f(x) \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right]. \end{aligned}\]The subscripts \(p\) and \(q\) show which distribution each expectation is taken with respect to. We have changed an expectation under \(p(x)\), which is hard to sample, into an expectation under \(q(x)\), which is easy to sample.

This gives the importance sampling estimator \[ \mathbb{E}_{p}[f] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} w(x^{(i)}) f(x^{(i)}), \] where \(x^{(i)} \sim q(x)\) and \(w(x) = p(x)/q(x)\) is the importance weight.

Points that are more likely under \(p(x)\) than under \(q(x)\) receive higher weights, and points that are less likely receive lower weights.

Handling Unnormalized Distributions

Like rejection sampling, importance sampling handles unnormalized distributions. Suppose that we know \(p(x)\) only up to a constant, \(p(x) = \tilde{p}(x)/Z_p\), where \(\tilde{p}(x)\) is the unnormalized density and \(Z_p = \int \tilde{p}(x) \mathrm{d}x\) is the normalization constant. Similarly, \(q(x) = \tilde{q}(x)/Z_q\). The tilde here marks an unnormalized density, unlike the normalized masses \(\tilde{p}_i\) of the grid approach.

The expectation becomes \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{p}[f] &= \frac{1}{Z_p} \int f(x) \tilde{p}(x) \mathrm{d}x \\ &= \frac{Z_q}{Z_p} \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[f(x) \frac{\tilde{p}(x)}{\tilde{q}(x)}\right]. \end{aligned}\]The second line uses \(\tilde{q}(x) = Z_q q(x)\). We do not need \(Z_p\) and \(Z_q\) separately. We need only their ratio, which the samples provide.

We can also write \(Z_p\) as \[\begin{aligned} Z_p &= \int \tilde{p}(x) \mathrm{d}x \\ &= Z_q \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\frac{\tilde{p}(x)}{\tilde{q}(x)}\right]. \end{aligned}\]Therefore \[\begin{aligned} \frac{Z_p}{Z_q} = \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\frac{\tilde{p}(x)}{\tilde{q}(x)}\right], \end{aligned}\] and we estimate this ratio with the samples from \(q(x)\) and the unnormalized weights \(\tilde{w}(x) = \tilde{p}(x)/\tilde{q}(x)\) \[\begin{aligned} \frac{Z_p}{Z_q} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\tilde{p}(x^{(i)})}{\tilde{q}(x^{(i)})} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}). \end{aligned}\]

The factor \(Z_q/Z_p\) is the inverse of the ratio that we just estimated. Substituting its estimate and the sample estimate of the expectation under \(q(x)\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{p}[f] &= \frac{Z_q}{Z_p} \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[f(x) \frac{\tilde{p}(x)}{\tilde{q}(x)}\right] \\ &\approx \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}) f(x^{(i)})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})}. \end{aligned}\]The factors \(1/N\) cancel. This is the self-normalized importance sampling estimator.

For the posterior, the normalization constant is the evidence \(p(\mathcal{D}) = \int p(\mathcal{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\) in the denominator of Bayes’ theorem. It is typically intractable, but the self-normalized estimator does not need it.

Understanding Efficiency Through Weights

The importance sampling estimator is valid for any proposal \(q(x)\) that covers the support of \(p(x)\), which means that \(q(x) > 0\) wherever \(p(x) \neq 0\). Its practical quality depends on how well \(q(x)\) approximates \(p(x)\).

If \(q(x)\) matches \(p(x)\), all importance weights are equal and all samples contribute equally. If the two distributions match only in part, some weights are larger than others, and the estimate relies on fewer samples.

The main problem is a proposal that undershoots the target, which means that it has too little probability mass where the target is high. There the weights \(w(x) = p(x)/q(x)\) can become very large. A few samples with very large weights can dominate the estimate, even when \(N\) is large.

12.6 Effective Sample Size

The effective sample size (ESS) measures how much information the weighted samples contain. Although we draw \(N\) samples from the proposal, the variance of the estimator can equal that of far fewer direct samples from \(p(x)\). We use the ESS to design good proposals and to find bad ones.

Intuitive Understanding

In a poll of public opinion, each person’s vote should carry about the same weight. If a few votes count as thousands and most votes count as fractions, a few people dominate the estimate. Even when we poll many people, the estimate is unreliable. Importance sampling has the same problem when a few samples have very large weights.

The ESS is the number of direct samples from \(p(x)\) that would give the same precision as our \(N\) weighted samples from \(q(x)\).

The Effective Sample Size Formula

The appendix derives the effective sample size from the variance of the self-normalized estimator, using approximations. The result, which does not depend on \(f\), is \[ \text{ESS} \approx \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}))^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})^2}, \] where \(\tilde{w}(x^{(i)})\) are the unnormalized importance weights.

The ESS is \(N\) times the ratio of the squared mean of the weights to the mean of their squares. It equals \(N\), the maximum, when all weights are equal. It decreases as the weights differ more, and it drops toward 1 when one weight dominates.

A Concrete Example

We estimate the mean of a standard normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) that is truncated to the region \([5,\infty)\). Truncation keeps only the part with \(x \geq 5\) and renormalizes it. The true mean is about 5.19. This could be the average brightness of the brightest stars in a population whose brightness follows a normal distribution.

The target distribution is \[ p(x) = \frac{\mathcal{N}(x|0,1) \cdot \mathbf{1}(x \geq 5)}{\int_{5}^{\infty} \mathcal{N}(t|0,1) \mathrm{d}t}, \] where \(\mathbf{1}(x \geq 5)\) is the indicator function, which equals 1 for \(x \geq 5\) and 0 otherwise. The numerator is \(\tilde{p}(x)\) and the integral in the denominator is \(Z_p\).

A naive proposal is the standard normal distribution, \(q(x) = \mathcal{N}(x|0,1)\). The unnormalized importance weights are then \[ \tilde{w}(x) = \frac{\mathcal{N}(x|0,1) \cdot \mathbf{1}(x \geq 5)}{\mathcal{N}(x|0,1)} = \mathbf{1}(x \geq 5). \]Only the samples that fall in \([5,\infty)\) have a non-zero weight. A sample from a standard normal distribution falls there with a probability of about \(2.87 \times 10^{-7}\), so we need millions of samples to obtain a few. With \(N = 10^7\) samples we expect about 3 samples with non-zero weights.

Suppose that 3 samples have non-zero weights. The unnormalized weights are \[ \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } i \in \{i_1, i_2, i_3\} \text{ (the 3 samples in } [5,\infty) \text{)} \\ 0 & \text{for all other } i .\end{cases} \]The ESS formula gives \[\begin{aligned} \text{ESS} &\approx \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}))^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})^2} \\ &= \frac{(1 + 1 + 1)^2}{1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2} \\ &= \frac{9}{3} = 3. \end{aligned}\]Here the ESS equals the number of samples with a non-zero weight. The ESS is limited by the rarity of the region of interest, so the estimator is very inefficient.

A better proposal puts more probability mass in the region of interest. For example, we can use an exponential distribution that is shifted to start at 5 \[ q(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda(x-5)} \cdot \mathbf{1}(x \geq 5), \] where \(\lambda > 0\) is a parameter. With this proposal, all samples fall in the region of interest \([5,\infty)\) and have non-zero weights. For \(\lambda = 3\) the proposal has a similar shape to the target in the region of interest, so the importance weights remain relatively balanced. For large \(N\) the sums in the ESS formula approach \(N\) times expectations under \(q(x)\), so \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\text{ESS}}{N} &\approx \frac{(\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2}{\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)^2]} \\ &= \frac{\left(\int_5^\infty \mathcal{N}(x|0,1)\,\mathrm{d}x\right)^2}{\int_5^\infty \mathcal{N}(x|0,1)^2/q(x)\,\mathrm{d}x} \approx \frac{(2.867 \times 10^{-7})^2}{1.014 \times 10^{-13}} \approx 0.81. \end{aligned}\]Here \(\tilde{w}(x) = \mathcal{N}(x|0,1)/q(x)\) on \([5,\infty)\), and numerical integration shows that the ESS is about 80% of \(N\).

Figure 12.5 compares the two proposals. A proposal that matches the target in the region of interest gives a smaller error in the estimated mean for the same \(N\). The shifted exponential proposal converges quickly with few samples, while the standard normal proposal needs billions of samples for a comparable error.

Practical Guidelines

When the ESS is small, the estimates have a high variance. The standard error of such an estimate, which is its standard deviation over repeated runs, scales as \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\text{ESS}})\) instead of \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})\). We therefore want a proposal with a high ESS.

When we choose a proposal, we follow four guidelines.

  • The support of \(q(x)\) must include the support of \(p(x)\).

  • Ideally \(q(x)\) is proportional to \(|f(x)|p(x)\), which minimizes the variance of the estimator \((1/N)\sum_{i=1}^{N} w(x^{(i)}) f(x^{(i)})\). The ESS does not depend on \(f\) and is largest for \(q(x) = p(x)\), whereas the choice above gives the lowest variance for one particular \(f\).

  • \(q(x)\) should have heavier tails than \(p(x)\) (Section 12.4), so that extreme weights in the tails do not reduce the effective sample size.

  • \(q(x)\) should be easy to sample from and to evaluate. Otherwise we gain little compared with sampling from \(p(x)\) directly.

Astronomical models often have dozens or hundreds of parameters. The grid approach and rejection sampling become impractical in many dimensions, because their computing time grows exponentially with the dimension. Importance sampling is also difficult in many dimensions, because a proposal that covers the target is hard to find. We describe Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods in Chapter 13. They generate correlated samples that explore the parameter space through local moves guided by the target distribution.

12.7 Appendix: Derivation of Effective Sample Size

This appendix derives the effective sample size formula for importance sampling. The derivation uses the delta method to analyze the variance of the self-normalized importance sampling estimator.

We start with our self-normalized importance sampling estimator \[ \hat{I} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}) f(x^{(i)})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})}. \]

For clarity, we define the normalized weights \[ w_i = \frac{\tilde{w}(x^{(i)})}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(j)})}, \] where the weights sum to 1, \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i = 1\). Our estimator becomes \[ \hat{I} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i f(x^{(i)}). \]

For comparison, suppose that we could sample directly from \(p(x)\). The variance of such a direct Monte Carlo estimator is \[ \text{Var}_{\text{direct}}(\hat{I}) = \frac{\text{Var}_p(f(x))}{N}, \]where \(\text{Var}_p\) is the variance under \(p(x)\). In the same way, \(\text{Var}_q\) and \(\text{Cov}_q\) below are the variance and covariance under \(q(x)\).

Variance by the Delta Method

Our self-normalized importance sampling estimator is a ratio of two random quantities \[ \hat{I} = \frac{A}{B}, \] where \[\begin{aligned} A &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})f(x^{(i)}) \\ B &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}). \end{aligned}\]

For large \(N\), both \(A\) and \(B\) converge to their expected values \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[A] &= \mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)f(x)] \\ \mathbb{E}[B] &= \mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)]. \end{aligned}\]

To derive the variance of our estimator \(\hat{I} = A/B\), we apply the delta method. The delta method approximates the variance of a function of random variables with a first-order Taylor expansion. We expand \(\hat{I} = A/B\) around the expected values \(\mathbb{E}[A]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[B]\) \[\begin{aligned} \hat{I} &\approx \frac{\mathbb{E}[A]}{\mathbb{E}[B]} + \frac{\partial}{\partial A}\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)\bigg|_{A=\mathbb{E}[A],B=\mathbb{E}[B]} (A - \mathbb{E}[A]) + \frac{\partial}{\partial B}\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)\bigg|_{A=\mathbb{E}[A],B=\mathbb{E}[B]} (B - \mathbb{E}[B]) \\ &= \frac{\mathbb{E}[A]}{\mathbb{E}[B]} + \frac{1}{\mathbb{E}[B]}(A - \mathbb{E}[A]) - \frac{\mathbb{E}[A]}{\mathbb{E}[B]^2}(B - \mathbb{E}[B]). \end{aligned}\]

We take the variance of this approximation and note that \(\mathbb{E}[A]/\mathbb{E}[B]\) is a constant \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(\hat{I}) &\approx \text{Var}\left(\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}[B]}(A - \mathbb{E}[A]) - \frac{\mathbb{E}[A]}{\mathbb{E}[B]^2}(B - \mathbb{E}[B])\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{\mathbb{E}[B]^2}\text{Var}(A) + \frac{\mathbb{E}[A]^2}{\mathbb{E}[B]^4}\text{Var}(B) - 2\frac{\mathbb{E}[A]}{\mathbb{E}[B]^3}\text{Cov}(A,B). \end{aligned}\]

Recalling that \(A = (1/N)\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})f(x^{(i)})\) and \(B = (1/N)\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})\), and that \(\mathbb{E}[A]/\mathbb{E}[B]\) equals \(\mathbb{E}_p[f]\), which we write as \(I\), we can express this in the original variables \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(\hat{I}) &\approx \frac{1}{N}\frac{\text{Var}_q(\tilde{w}(x)f(x)) + I^2\text{Var}_q(\tilde{w}(x)) - 2I\text{Cov}_q(\tilde{w}(x)f(x),\tilde{w}(x))}{(\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2} \\ &= \frac{1}{N}\frac{\text{Var}_q(\tilde{w}(x)f(x) - I \cdot \tilde{w}(x))}{(\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2}. \end{aligned}\]The last step uses \(\text{Var}(X-Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) - 2\text{Cov}(X,Y)\), where \(X = \tilde{w}(x)f(x)\) and \(Y = I \cdot \tilde{w}(x)\).

This formula shows how the uncertainty in both the numerator and the denominator of our estimator contributes to the overall variance. The term \(\tilde{w}(x)f(x) - I\,\tilde{w}(x)\) equals \(\tilde{w}(x)(f(x) - I)\). Its mean under \(q(x)\) is \(\mathbb{E}[A] - I\,\mathbb{E}[B]\), which is zero. Its variance is therefore the mean of its square.

The variance of the estimator becomes \[ \text{Var}(\hat{I}) \approx \frac{1}{N} \frac{\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)^2 (f(x) - I)^2]}{(\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2}. \]

Equating the Variances

To find the effective sample size, we set this variance equal to the variance of direct sampling \[ \frac{\text{Var}_p(f(x))}{\text{ESS}} = \frac{1}{N} \frac{\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)^2 (f(x) - I)^2]}{(\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2}. \]

Solving for the ESS gives \[ \text{ESS} = N \frac{\text{Var}_p(f(x)) \cdot (\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2}{\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)^2 (f(x) - I)^2]}. \]

Since we typically do not know \(\text{Var}_p(f(x))\) and \(f(x)\) differs between applications, we derive a function-independent approximation. We replace \((f(x) - I)^2\) in the denominator by its mean under \(p(x)\), which is \(\text{Var}_p(f(x))\). This treats \((f(x) - I)^2\) as unrelated to the weights, and \(\text{Var}_p(f(x))\) cancels. The result is \[ \text{ESS} \approx N \frac{(\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)])^2}{\mathbb{E}_q[\tilde{w}(x)^2]}. \]

Using sample estimates, this becomes \[ \text{ESS} \approx N \frac{(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}))^2}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})^2} = \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)}))^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde{w}(x^{(i)})^2}. \]

12.8 Tutorial: Sampling Stellar Masses

Astronomers often need random samples from a distribution that standard generators do not cover, to simulate a population or to explore a posterior. This tutorial draws stellar masses from the initial mass function (IMF). It uses the three methods of this chapter, inversion of the cumulative distribution function (CDF), rejection sampling and importance sampling. The full tutorial can be found at https://statml.org/ as tutorial 12.

The IMF is the distribution of stellar masses at birth. A star’s mass sets its luminosity, its lifetime and the elements it returns to the gas. The IMF therefore shapes how a stellar population shines, ages and enriches its surroundings. We cannot observe it directly, partly because massive stars die young. Astronomers instead simulate populations from a model IMF and compare them with observations, which needs many random masses.

The most direct route inverts the CDF, the probability of a mass below a given value (Section 12.3). Each uniform random number from the computer then maps to one mass. Below one solar mass the IMF is a power law in each of a few mass ranges. The CDF of a power law inverts in closed form. Every random number gives an exact mass, and the histogram in Figure 12.6a follows the IMF.

Many distributions have no CDF that we can invert, and rejection sampling needs only the density (Section 12.4). It draws candidates from a simpler proposal, here a decaying exponential scaled to lie above the IMF, and keeps those that fall under the IMF. The closer the proposal follows the IMF, the fewer candidates are discarded for each sample that we keep. Its samples follow the same IMF as those of the inversion.

Some questions need an average over the IMF rather than samples, such as the mean mass, which turns a star count into a total mass. Importance sampling estimates such an average from a convenient proposal and weights each sample by the ratio of the IMF to the proposal (Section 12.5). As in rejection sampling, the proposal matters. Where it lies far below the IMF, a few large weights dominate the estimate. The effective sample size (ESS) counts how many direct draws from the IMF the weighted samples are worth (Section 12.6).

The tutorial compares an exponential and a uniform proposal. The exponential proposal roughly follows the IMF, while the uniform one lies far below it at low masses, where most stars are (Figure 12.6a). The uniform weights therefore vary widely, and the exponential weights stay closer to equal (Figure 12.6b). The exponential proposal keeps the larger ESS, as the labels show.

All three methods turn uniform random numbers into samples of a distribution that we care about. Inversion is exact when the CDF inverts, and otherwise the proposal decides how efficient the sampling is. The same choice returns for posteriors that we can write down but not sample directly (Chapter 13). There the ESS tells us how many independent samples a weighted estimate is worth.

Further Reading

Von Neumann (1951) described rejection sampling and other ways to generate random numbers. Box and Muller (1958) turned uniform random numbers into normally distributed ones without inverting the normal CDF. Forsythe (1972) generalized von Neumann’s method of comparing random numbers. Kinderman and Monahan (1977) introduced a rejection method based on the ratio of uniform random numbers. Marsaglia (1977) described the squeeze method, which adds simple bounds that save evaluations of the density. Goertzel (1949), Kahn (1950) and Kahn and Harris (1951) applied early importance sampling to particle transport. Kahn and Marshall (1953) presented importance sampling as a way to reduce variance, and Kahn (1955) discussed such techniques. Rubinstein (1981), Kalos and Whitlock (1986) and Fishman (1996) wrote books on Monte Carlo methods. Devroye (1986) covers random number generation. Kroupa (2001) gave the IMF we sample.
